item.title: O, Miami redefined what a poetry festival can be Miami 5 min read
item.description:
• Daniel Rivero

Overview

On April 22, 2014, a strangely familiar man rode a white horse down Calle Ocho, the heart of Cuban Miami. The man was an actor, hired to portray Cuban national hero and acclaimed poet José Martí. Martí died in 1898, but as his reincarnated likeness passed, helpers handed out white roses bearing his poems.

As the horse trudged on, unsuspecting elderly Cubans gathered to witness the unlikely event. Many recited lines of poetry they had learned in childhood.

“These viejitos were following us as we’re all walking down Calle Ocho. And then – my parents coming, my grandmother getting the roses. Something happened there,” says Melody Santiago Cummings, executive director of O, Miami. “I felt changed.”

Welcome to O, Miami –– possibly the world’s most inventive and dynamic poetry festival.

Seamlessly dovetailing between the whimsical and the heartfelt, the festival has become a Miami institution since it rose up from the ashes of a city that was a major epicenter of the 2008 financial crisis.

As families lost homes and businesses shuttered, the city experienced a renaissance driven by artists and visionaries eager to activate the sudden surplus of inexpensive studio space.

In 2009, Knight Foundation provided seed funding to an experimental poetry project, the University of Wynwood, the brainchild of poet and essayist P. Scott Cunningham. Three years later, Knight funded O, Miami, a citywide poetry festival, the natural outgrowth of that early experiment.

Unlike most poetry festivals, there was not one venue, one ticket, one wristband. Instead, The O, Miami festival named an impossible-sounding mission that it pursued with creativity and flair: to ensure that everyone in Miami encountered a poem during April, National Poetry Month.

All manner of poetry events have been held over the ensuing annual festivals. There have been readings by emerging and established poets, yes. But also, poetry has found itself embedded in events like a Poetry Is Dead mock funeral procession, athletic competitions, oyster tastings, underwater poetry in a hotel pool, a poetry-themed remake of 2 Fast 2 Furious and a Bad Bunny lookalike contest.

  • Photo credit: Gesi Schilling
  • Caroline Cabrera and Melody Santiago Cummings. Photo credit: Gesi Schilling.

Places where Miamians have encountered poetry:

  • Fruit stickers in supermarkets
  • Pints of ice cream
  • Girl Scout cookies
  • Freshly poured concrete sidewalks
  • Urinals
  • Miami Metrorail tickets
  • Airplane banners
  • Bus stops
  • Labels stitched into T-Shirts on store racks
  • Two rooftops visible to travelers flying in and out of Miami International Airport
  • Sandwiches
  • Beach sand

In 2019 Knight provided a major non-project grant that helped O, Miami plant deeper roots as an organization that could look towards the future. By then, the once-affordable real estate market of the festival’s early days had swelled into one of the most expensive in the nation, putting pressure on O, Miami and other cultural organizations.

“You don’t want your success to be totally reliant on one funder –– and I think we’ve been able to mature out of that –– but had it not been for Knight, we would not be here,” says Santiago Cummings.

In recent years, the festival has expanded significantly, evolving into a year-round organization. Teachers across South Florida now incorporate poetry into their classrooms using O, Miami’s Sunroom curriculum. An annual summer apprenticeship program has become an incubator for artists of all mediums. The organization regularly publishes books, ranging from poetry to prose, from quirky poetry about Miami’s weird side to children’s books and anthologies tackling transportation, climate change and gun violence.

The team has also begun to offer creative services to local governments and businesses, helping fill funding gaps while advancing its mission. Storefronts and construction sites throughout the city now routinely feature poetry written by South Florida residents.

“Our problem is that we do too much to effectively tell the story of who we are and what we do,” jokes artistic director Caroline Cabrera.

Impact at a glance

Since 2011…

  • 875 events or projects produced
  • 30 titles published
  • 2,755 Miami-Dade County students served
  • Dozens of classroom poetry anthologies distributed
  • More than 42,000 poems collected

In 2025 alone…

  • More than 150 events held in four languages
  • Eighteen artists mentored
  • 56 poems displayed on windows and storefronts
  • Thousands of books sold
  • 9,000 poetry fruit stickers placed on produce in three languages
  • 90 pounds of plastic recycled into poetry
  • 410 linear feet of poetry fences installed throughout Miami
  • 466 poems exchanged for bread

The Impact

  • 875

    Events or projects produced since 2011

  • 2,755

    Miami-Dade County students served

  • 90

    Pounds of plastic recycled into poetry in 2025

  • Photo credit: Gesi Schilling
  • Photo credit: Gesi Schilling

During April, the festival really does feel like it is everywhere. A decade-and-a-half partnership with public radio station WLRN means poems are broadcast to commuters during rush hour throughout the month. The collaboration also spawned an entirely new poetry form: the ZipOde.

In a ZipOde, the numbers in a given zip code determine the number of words in a line, and the resulting poem must be about that specific place. Public radio listeners began submitting ZipOdes in 2015; to date, more than 20,000 poems have been collected. An anthology published on the tenth anniversary of the ZipOde pairs poems collected over the years with photography.

ZipOdes have spread across the country, with versions of the poetry form and related events have popped up in Massachusetts, Ohio, Maryland and beyond.

The key to O, Miami’s success is a deeply felt love for its namesake city, in all of its diversity.

“We are a placemaking organization,” says Cabrera. “If an idea can spark a conversation about this place or lead to true moments of self-expression in this space and celebrate it in all its complexity, we will entertain it.”

Daniel Rivero is an investigative reporter with WLRN Public Radio in Miami. How work has been featured in the Miami Herald, NPR, the Guardian, ABC News and other outlets. His first book, Just Freedom: Inside Florida’s Decades-Long Voting Rights Battle, was published in 2025.

“We are a placemaking organization. If an idea can spark a conversation about this place or lead to true moments of self-expression in this space and celebrate it in all its complexity, we will entertain it.”

item.title: What it takes to paint at monumental scale, with Sydney James Detroit 5 min read
item.description:
• Ashley Simon

Overview

Sydney G. James is a Detroit-born and Detroit-based fine arts painter and muralist whose large-scale public works and studio practice explore Black identity, representation and community. She earned a BFA from the College for Creative Studies and began her career as an art director in advertising before expanding into visual art in film and television in Los Angeles. James returned to Detroit in 2011 and has since completed murals locally and across the globe, including the acclaimed Girl With the D Earring in the North End.

She was awarded a 2017 Kresge Arts in Detroit Fellowship and co-founded the BLKOUT Walls street mural festival, creating platforms for diverse artists. Her work has been exhibited at institutions including the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit and the Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, as well as galleries such as Detroit Artists Market, Red Bull House of Art and Janice Charach Gallery.

Q&A

When you’re starting something like this, what’s the very first thing you have to do? Where does it all begin?

The first thing I do is research. I look at the location—what it is, what it was, and how it’s structured. I ask the basic questions: who, what, where and why.

With The Girl with the D Earring, that meant really spending time in the North End. There’s a lot of history there, especially around Black life and Black presence in the neighborhood. I wanted to understand the people in the area and what that place actually is.

The building itself—the Chroma building—was originally a cold storage facility, so that history mattered too. I often use compositions that already exist in pop culture. In this case, it was The Girl with the Pearl Earring. The “D” comes from the Detroit Tigers logo, but it’s also bigger than that—it’s the branding of Detroit.

Community engagement is important to me, especially with public work. I want it to be a two-way conversation between the artist and the people who live around it. The work should feel enjoyable and relatable to the community.

When I was contacted to work on the Ralph C. Wilson site, there were a few things I had to consider right away. The structure is unique—it’s a ventilation system. It’s also owned by Canada and visible from Canada. Because of that, it couldn’t just work from one angle. It had to be a full 360 experience. You have to think about who can see it and how far away they are.

Once I do the homework, I start drawing. For Ralph C. Wilson, I listed out ideas of what people can actually do and enjoy in a public park. I wanted to draw something that works whether you’re young or old, able-bodied or disabled. And everybody can enjoy bubbles. It’s something people can experience together.

I also like to put little Easter eggs in my work. Inside the bubbles, there are small silhouettes showing different ways to get to Canada—the tunnel, the bridge. It’s a simple composition, but it says a lot. You don’t have to put the kitchen sink in there.

What tools, skills, or supports do you absolutely rely on to make this work possible?

The tools change with the job. Going back to Ralph C. Wilson, for example, you can’t do something like that alone. You need people. You need relationships—especially with lift rental companies. They come out, review the site and tell you exactly what equipment you’ll need. A lot of the time, you’re gauging a project based on what you’ve done before.

With The Girl with the D Earring, I worked with a team of six people and we finished it in about five and a half days. I thought it would be the same with Ralph C Wilson Park—ha!—but I didn’t fully account for the scale. It’s about 2000 sq ft larger than Girl with the D Earring because of the size and the 360-degree nature of it.

I also have Sherwin-Williams come out to help estimate how much paint I’m going to need. Big projects need big equipment and big tools.

Smaller projects are different. For those, I used mural paint by Chroma. It’s a more liquid outdoor–indoor acrylic with really great coverage.

No matter the tools, though, I want you to be able to recognize my work. The tools can change, but the voice should still be there.

What would you say is the most difficult part of the work that demands the most from you mentally or logistically?

It’s physical. I don’t care if you’re on a small wall or a huge wall. Mural artists aren’t blue-collar or white-collar—we’re just collared. We have to be trained on the equipment like any other construction worker. We need the same certifications and the same insurance.

It’s physically challenging, and it’s mentally challenging too, because you’re often isolated. You might be standing for hours. It’s intensive labor. That’s the part a lot of people don’t see or understand, because art is so—art is so beautiful.

What’s one mistake or failure that taught you something important or essential?

Whatever happens on this planet—good or terrible—there are lessons everywhere. With the Ralph C. Wilson Park project, I had a huge mess up with the UV protection coating . The product wasn’t mixed properly and it sprayed on very thick and uneven.. An hour later,  it rained hard. The following day, I woke up to a text from someone at the park with photos attached, asking, “Is this supposed to look like that?” It didn’t look right at all. There was a thick foggy film covering my painting; specifically the biggest face on the painting. It was so frustrating because we’d already put a lot of work in. That moment taught me patience. Step away. If you’re unsure or feeling overwhelmed, don’t come back angry. Take a beat, take care of yourself, and then come back with a solution.

How do you stay sane? What helps keep your perspective or keep you grounded when things become overwhelming?

I always remind myself that everything turns out ok. Everything is fixable. I can’t control how other people treat me or perceive me, but I can control how I respond.

What’s one book that you think everyone should read?

E.M. Forster’s science fiction short story The Machine Stops. Everybody should read it.

item.title: What it takes to run a public library, with Maureen Hartman St. Paul 5 min read
item.description:
• Ricardo Mor

Overview

Maureen Hartman is the Director of Saint Paul Public Library, overseeing one of the most dynamic public library systems in the country: 250 team members across 13 locations and a mobile library that received over 1.2 million visits in 2025.

Since joining SPPL in 2017 as Deputy Director for Public Services, Hartman has driven changes that have reshaped how the system connects with its community, from eliminating late fines to guiding a $35 million Transforming Libraries initiative to modernize branches citywide, to which Knight Foundation contributed $2 million. We spoke with Hartman about what it takes to run a library system as ambitious as Saint Paul’s.

Q&A

When you’re starting something like this, what’s the very first thing you have to do? Where does it all begin?

As a kid, my family had a regular practice of going to the library at least weekly. It was just a regular habit in my family.

I went to college, got a liberal arts degree, majored in English. I graduated and had a bunch of different jobs, and I thought, what am I going to do next? I was living down the street from, ironically, a Saint Paul public library. I remembered how much I liked the idea of libraries and how much I like reading. So I submitted an application to be a volunteer.

I still tell this story today even though I’m kind of embarrassed by it. I was not a good volunteer. I quit. The job that they gave me was cleaning the covers of the picture books. It was so boring. It made me start looking into what it takes to work in public libraries. I decided to get my master’s degree in library science.

What I found out as I entered the field is that it wasn’t exactly as I imagined, but I was really good at it and I really loved it. People think libraries are about books. But they are, in fact, about people.

“People think libraries are about books. But they are, in fact, about people.”

What tools, skills or supports do you absolutely rely on to make this work possible?

You have to like working with people. That’s true of anyone who works in a public library, but it could not be more true of the leader of the organization.

The second part is a passion and a love and understanding of community. The community is the whole reason. We have to love our community, but we also have to be in conversation with community members about our services, so they can continue to evolve.

And adaptive leadership. I learned this most importantly in my career leading the library through COVID. We are in the mix on issues like AI, community-first public safety, intellectual freedom, and privacy. Almost any issue that we are facing or challenged by in our world today happens inside the library.

What’s the toughest part of this work — the thing that demands the most from you mentally or logistically?

The hardest part is when there are challenges outside of our control that are impacting our ability to provide good service. Some of those challenges are budget related. Some might be challenges such as mental health issues or fentanyl addiction increase. When it’s outside of our control, that’s a big challenge. But we use the tools that we have, which are bringing people to the table and problem solving together.

Also, there’s still a lot of education about what public libraries do now. Sometimes we’re left out of important community conversations when we know we have an important role to play. Part of this job is educating people about what libraries do now and seeing the different ways people are using libraries.

Who do you lean on? How did you build the team or partnerships that make this real?

I put a lot of trust in my senior leadership team. I am influenced by some language from Brené Brown about who’s in the arena with you. I am very vulnerable, very honest with that team about both the incredible work that we’re doing, but our challenges as well. I can’t imagine leading any kind of organization without a strong team.

What’s one mistake or failure that taught you something essential?

It’s better to be done than perfect. We have a tendency to overbuild things. In the library profession, we want it to be 100% perfect before we launch it. We’ve brought design thinking into the library to help folks more rapidly prototype something, get the feedback and then launch it.

What helps you keep perspective or stay grounded when the work gets overwhelming?

During COVID, I started going to restorative yoga on Wednesday nights and I never miss one.

You have to have people you can laugh with, and I’m really proud that my leadership team remains that. My family keeps me really grounded. I have two teenagers and a spouse. Sometimes when I convert a story that wasn’t funny into a funny story for them, it helps me put it in perspective and move on.

One book everyone should read

Holes by Louis Sachar. As I was studying to be a librarian and as I was entering my library career, this was the book I recommended the most. When this book came out, I would have kids come up to me — middle school boys who aren’t usually the ones coming up to ask for recommendations — and they would just say, “Do you have any other books like Holes?” It became a guiding question for my library, thinking about the folks that are in libraries or want to engage with reading but don’t know where to start. And it gave me the opportunity to really dig into my work with teenagers and try to put the right book in the hands of every kid.

Since joining SPPL in 2017 as Deputy Director for Public Services, Hartman has driven changes that have reshaped how the system connects with its community, from eliminating late fines to guiding a $35 million Transforming Libraries initiative to modernize branches citywide, to which Knight Foundation contributed $2 million. We spoke with Hartman about what it takes to run a library system as ambitious as Saint Paul’s.

Q&A

When you’re starting something like this, what’s the very first thing you have to do? Where does it all begin?

As a kid, my family had a regular practice of going to the library at least weekly. It was just a regular habit in my family.

I went to college, got a liberal arts degree, majored in English. I graduated and had a bunch of different jobs, and I thought, what am I going to do next? I was living down the street from, ironically, a Saint Paul public library. I remembered how much I liked the idea of libraries and how much I like reading. So I submitted an application to be a volunteer.

I still tell this story today even though I’m kind of embarrassed by it. I was not a good volunteer. I quit. The job that they gave me was cleaning the covers of the picture books. It was so boring. It made me start looking into what it takes to work in public libraries. I decided to get my master’s degree in library science.

What I found out as I entered the field is that it wasn’t exactly as I imagined, but I was really good at it and I really loved it. People think libraries are about books. But they are, in fact, about people.

“People think libraries are about books. But they are, in fact, about people.”

What tools, skills or supports do you absolutely rely on to make this work possible?

You have to like working with people. That’s true of anyone who works in a public library, but it could not be more true of the leader of the organization.

The second part is a passion and a love and understanding of community. The community is the whole reason. We have to love our community, but we also have to be in conversation with community members about our services, so they can continue to evolve.

And adaptive leadership. I learned this most importantly in my career leading the library through COVID. We are in the mix on issues like AI, community-first public safety, intellectual freedom, and privacy. Almost any issue that we are facing or challenged by in our world today happens inside the library.

What’s the toughest part of this work — the thing that demands the most from you mentally or logistically?

The hardest part is when there are challenges outside of our control that are impacting our ability to provide good service. Some of those challenges are budget related. Some might be challenges such as mental health issues or fentanyl addiction increase. When it’s outside of our control, that’s a big challenge. But we use the tools that we have, which are bringing people to the table and problem solving together.

Also, there’s still a lot of education about what public libraries do now. Sometimes we’re left out of important community conversations when we know we have an important role to play. Part of this job is educating people about what libraries do now and seeing the different ways people are using libraries.

Who do you lean on? How did you build the team or partnerships that make this real?

I put a lot of trust in my senior leadership team. I am influenced by some language from Brené Brown about who’s in the arena with you. I am very vulnerable, very honest with that team about both the incredible work that we’re doing, but our challenges as well. I can’t imagine leading any kind of organization without a strong team.

What’s one mistake or failure that taught you something essential?

It’s better to be done than perfect. We have a tendency to overbuild things. In the library profession, we want it to be 100% perfect before we launch it. We’ve brought design thinking into the library to help folks more rapidly prototype something, get the feedback and then launch it.

What helps you keep perspective or stay grounded when the work gets overwhelming?

During COVID, I started going to restorative yoga on Wednesday nights and I never miss one.

You have to have people you can laugh with, and I’m really proud that my leadership team remains that. My family keeps me really grounded. I have two teenagers and a spouse. Sometimes when I convert a story that wasn’t funny into a funny story for them, it helps me put it in perspective and move on.

One book everyone should read

Holes by Louis Sachar. As I was studying to be a librarian and as I was entering my library career, this was the book I recommended the most. When this book came out, I would have kids come up to me — middle school boys who aren’t usually the ones coming up to ask for recommendations — and they would just say, “Do you have any other books like Holes?” It became a guiding question for my library, thinking about the folks that are in libraries or want to engage with reading but don’t know where to start. And it gave me the opportunity to really dig into my work with teenagers and try to put the right book in the hands of every kid.

item.title: What it takes to revitalize a downtown area, with Erin Keller Macon 7 min read
item.description:
• Mark Glaser

Overview

Erin Keller is a fundraising and nonprofit development professional specializing in donations, grants and capital campaigns. A Mercer University alumna and former women’s basketball standout, she has a Master’s in Higher Education Leadership and multiple nonprofit leadership credentials. At NewTown Macon, Keller is the chief of staff and vice president for development, focusing on donor engagement, fundraising strategy and special program leadership, all while staying deeply connected to her community.

NewTown has led one of the most significant downtown revitalization efforts in the country. Keller explains what it takes to revitalize a downtown area in this profile, based on her work in Macon.

Q&A

When you’re starting something like this, what’s the very first thing you have to do? Where does it all begin?

I think it’s a love of people and a love of place. There are people who can move from place to place and do the same work. I personally cannot do that. It’s my community development, economic development mantras: love the people, love the place.

I was in my late 20s when I started working here. So there was still a lot for me to figure out. Our late CEO Josh Rogers was not much older than I was, but he was definitely an older soul. He was very firm in who he was, what he was about and what his work was. What he was devoting his life to and his life’s mission. And so it’s really easy to get on board and to fall in love with something when that type of person is the one leading you.

And it also just allows you to be really creative. Ten years ago, I can’t tell you that I even knew what community development really looked like or was, but it is something different every day. No year is like another. And so I’ve achieved a lot of professional accomplishments, because this work is just so diverse, and to see your work in a tangible way is also really inspiring.

What tools, skills, or supports do you absolutely rely on to make this work possible?

So much of this work is intuitive, being able to articulate a vision and reason for different strategies we might do. In terms of support, this staff is great. We work very collaboratively. So part of all of our success is the power of team. In meetings, Josh told us we could solve any problem with the people around this table. And we believe that to this day.

It might take us a little longer since he’s not next to us, but that is the culture that he built. And so the support or tools always seem to come from this office, or from external regional and national resources that actually have advanced our work, accelerated our work. Between that and our other philanthropic support systems, we’ve had the resources to do creative solutions and problem-solving tactics that are mission critical to getting us to our vision and mission.

What would you say is the most difficult part of the work that demands the most from you mentally or logistically?

It’s hard for some people to believe that we’re truly altruistic. I understand that that’s the world that we live in, but sometimes people think the things that we implement or are advocates for automatically are things to pad NewTown’s pockets. Economic development is not something that is easily understood by the general public. People’s perception is their reality, so it’s important to be able to communicate effectively, and give a reason why we’re doing what we’re doing.

Macon is a tale of two cities, depending upon your ZIP code, which affects your health expectancy, your education and your wages. So I can understand how a shining downtown does not resonate with many people. But when you’re trying to have those conversations with people, that’s hard. That’s really hard, because sometimes it’s just not going to click.

Who do you lean on through your team or partnerships to help make this happen?

In terms of strategic partnerships, I lean on the Macon-Bibb County Urban Development Authority and Alex Morrison — he’s the executive director there. We’re doing some of the same work, but we’re on the private side. And so instead of competition, it’s become more collaborative. They are integral to NewTown’s success because a lot of what we’re doing is the right hand and left hand. That partnership is invaluable.

And in terms of the personal, I really rely on my co-workers a lot. Staff meetings are great for us to find solutions. Whenever I have an issue, I might go to different people depending upon what it is, but working with this type of team that is collaborative, fairly altruistic and passionate about what we do, it’s an anomaly among workplaces. I’m so thankful for it, because it really just makes it more enjoyable to come to work. Having the support of the people alongside you every day — that’s a blessing beyond measure.

What's one mistake or failure that taught you something important or essential?

There was one instance with one of the board members, it was in a meeting setting. It was getting out of hand, and I could not reel it back in. And I just stopped talking, which is very hard for me to do. Was that the most professional? Absolutely not. And then they would ask me a question, and I didn’t have anything to say.

I learned a lot about myself then. One thing was emotional regulation. I probably should have left and come back to regroup, to be productive, as opposed to trying to solve it like a child. And also being able to make a phone call, admit when you’re wrong, and then figuring out how we’re going to move forward to communicate better.

I think we learned a lot about each other, but that was definitely a humbling experience, and also taught me a lot. It comes easier to me now, after many years, but in the beginning, it was rough, but it was a good lesson.

How do you stay sane? What helps keep your perspective or keep you grounded when things become overwhelming?

I’m a verbal processor, and thank God that my colleagues are also verbal processors. And then also just taking a beat, processing, but then also having a moment. So some yoga helps. Just trying to remind myself not to be so reactive, because it can get a little overwhelming.

We’re doing a lot of good stuff, and there are a lot of plates spinning in the air, but I think just being able to sometimes take a walk downtown and remember what this used to be and give myself a second to dream what it could be again. When I have some tough days, I watch Simon Sinek’s TED Talk, “Start with Why.” It’s very good, just to ground yourself and think that ‘that is a moment; it won’t last forever.’

Knowing your why brings you back to the work that we’re doing and the vision we have and staying true to the mission. And at some point, you have to cut out the noise.

What’s one book that you think everyone should read?

“Happy City” by Charles Montgomery. It’s really about the intersection of happiness and urban design. And it gives you case studies of different cities that have planned differently. Especially for Americans, we don’t get enough exercise. We’re in cars all day, and what tends to make people happiest in a community is social trust. I think that is very true of the downtown community. I think that they’re not perfect, but I think generally people are very trusting, and so people enjoy living and working here and socializing here.

In suburbia, we’re less likely to get to know each other when our houses are far apart, with long driveways from the road and a lack of sidewalks, or because you have to drive everywhere. If you live downtown, though, you’re more likely to walk places, smile at people on the street, things of that nature. So I felt like that was a really good foundation for the type of community that I would like to live in. Working at NewTown has taught me the importance of not just living in a community, but being part of a community.
